Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

Question: Which person or organization did Donald Groves work for?

His expertise and dedication to medical research have been invaluable to our institution." A review of Groves' publications and presentations reveals a significant body of work conducted during his tenure at Stony Brook University Hospital. His research focused on innovative treatments and therapies, which have improved patient outcomes and saved countless lives. Dr. Kenneth Kaushansky, Dean of the Renaissance School of Medicine at Stony Brook University, praised Groves' contributions, saying, "Donald's work has been instrumental in shaping the future of healthcare. His collaboration with our hospital has led to numerous breakthroughs, and we are grateful for his contributions." Data from the hospital's records and academic journals corroborate Groves' affiliation with Stony Brook University Hospital. A search of the National Institutes of Health's (NIH) database reveals multiple grants awarded to Groves during his time at the hospital, totaling over $1 million in funding. These grants supported research projects focused on cutting-edge medical technologies and treatments. In an interview, Dr. Groves himself acknowledged his association with Stony Brook University Hospital, stating, "My time at Stony Brook was incredibly rewarding. Document 2: **Breaking News**

Renowned Researcher Donald Groves Leaves Lasting Legacy at University of Washington

Seattle, WA - The academic community is mourning the loss of Donald Groves, a trailblazing researcher who spent over two decades at the University of Washington, leaving an indelible mark on the institution. Groves, a pioneer in his field, dedicated his career to advancing our understanding of complex systems and pushing the boundaries of human knowledge. During his tenure at UW, Groves authored numerous groundbreaking papers, earning him international recognition and accolades. His work on nonlinear dynamics and chaos theory has been cited over 10,000 times, making him one of the most influential researchers of his generation. "Donald was a giant in his field," said Dr. Maria Rodriguez, a colleague and friend of Groves. "His passion for discovery was contagious, and he inspired a generation of students and researchers to pursue careers in science." Groves' impact extended beyond the academic sphere. His research has been applied in various industries, from climate modeling to medical diagnostics. His work on pattern recognition, for instance, has been used to develop more accurate weather forecasting systems. "Donald's contributions to our understanding of complex systems have been instrumental in improving our ability to predict and prepare for natural disasters," said Dr. John Taylor, a researcher at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). "His legacy will continue to inspire and inform our work for years to come." Groves' dedication to his craft was matched only by his commitment to mentoring and teaching. He supervised over 50 graduate students and postdoctoral researchers during his time at UW, many of whom have gone on to become leading researchers in their own right. "Don was more than just an advisor; he was a mentor, a friend, and a role model," said Dr. Sophia Patel, a former student of Groves who is now a researcher at NASA. "He instilled in us a sense of curiosity and a passion for discovery that will stay with us for the rest of our careers." Groves' passing leaves a void in the academic community, but his work and legacy will continue to inspire and influence generations of researchers to come.
